name: DEFAME
purpose: Multimodal fact-verification framework that plans and executes a sequence of tools — web search, reverse image search, image forensics, geolocation — against an image-plus-text claim and produces a verdict with an evidence trail.
journalism_use_case: Verification of image-plus-text claims as they actually circulate on social media, where the claim is a photo with a caption. Its distinguishing output is a tool-by-tool evidence trail a journalist can audit, rather than a bare label.
pros: Addresses the real shape of modern misinformation — captioned images — which text-only fact-verification systems structurally cannot handle
The auditable per-tool evidence trail is the right design: a reporter can see which step produced which signal rather than trusting an end-to-end score
Apache-2.0 with a tagged release (v2.1.0, 2025-04-17) and Dockerised deployment
Architecturally modular, so the orchestration pattern is reusable even if you replace the default components
cons: NOT local by default: claim text and submitted images are sent to the configured LLM provider (GPT-4o by default) and to external search and reverse-image services — a disclosure for any unpublished image
Research prototype: verdicts and the evidence chain are probabilistic model output requiring human adjudication, never proof; the image-forensics and geolocation outputs are leads, not determinations
Activity has slowed (pushed 2026-05-21, release April 2025) and the community is small (62 stars), so you would own any maintenance
Requires API keys for an LLM and for search/reverse-image tools, so operating cost is per-use and depends on third parties
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the hosted-LLM default (GPT-4o) and required API keys are stated in the project's own configuration documentation; 62 stars with 4 open issues indicates a research release with limited uptake.
assessment: The most interesting architecture in this subcategory and the one I would study before building anything similar — tool-orchestration with an auditable trail is the right pattern for verification automation. But I would not deploy it as shipped, because the default configuration sends source images to OpenAI and to Yandex-class reverse-search engines. For your profile the viable path is to reimplement the orchestration against a self-hosted model and local forensics (Sherloq, PhotoHolmes) for sensitive material, and use DEFAME as-is only on already-public images.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-05-21, latest release v2.1.0 (2025-04-17), 62 stars, 4 open issues. Six months since last push and nineteen months since the last release; academic-lab release pattern. Declining rather than dormant since commits continued into 2026.
model_or_data_licence: n/a by default — uses hosted LLMs (GPT-4o default); optional local GPU components pull third-party models whose licences were not verified.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. The operative constraints are the third-party API terms for the LLM and search services.
costs: Software free. Operation requires paid API keys: an LLM provider (GPT-4o-class token charges) plus search and reverse-image services — per-claim cost, rates not verified here. Optional CUDA GPU for local components. Real cost is per-use, not infrastructure.
privacy: NOT local by default. Claim text and submitted images go to the configured LLM provider and to external search and reverse-image services. Unsuitable for unpublished or source-supplied imagery without reconfiguration to local components.
alternatives: InVID-WeVerify plugin for a journalist-usable (also non-local) equivalent
PhotoHolmes plus Sherloq plus ShadowFinder for a fully local manual workflow
Reimplementing the orchestration pattern against a self-hosted model
blockers: Hosted LLM and external search by default — images and claims leave your infrastructure
summary: Multimodal fact-verification framework that plans and executes a sequence of tools — web search, reverse image search…

name: FacTool
purpose: Framework for detecting factual errors in generated text across scenarios (knowledge-based QA, code, maths, scientific review) by extracting claims, collecting evidence and scoring factuality.
journalism_use_case: Auditing AI-generated or AI-assisted copy before publication — the practical question of whether a draft produced with model assistance contains invented facts — and as a reusable claim-extraction-plus-evidence-collection component inside a newsroom verification pipeline.
pros: Framed honestly as error detection in generated text rather than adjudication of public claims, which is the correct and narrower problem
Multi-scenario design (including code and maths) makes it useful for auditing a wider range of AI-assisted outputs than prose alone
Apache-2.0 and architecturally clear, so the claim-extraction stage is reusable in isolation
cons: NOT local: requires an OpenAI API key and a search API (Serper or Google) for the knowledge-QA scenario, so submitted text, extracted claims and generated queries go to third parties
Dormant: last push 2024-08-19, no releases or tags, 937 stars with 24 open issues — initial interest that did not sustain maintenance
Outputs are probabilistic factuality signals for triage, not conclusive verification; the paper's own framing is error detection, which users routinely over-read
Tied to specific providers, so substituting a self-hosted model requires code changes
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the required OpenAI and search API keys stated in the README; no activity since August 2024; 937 stars with 24 open issues.
assessment: The use case — checking AI-assisted copy for invented facts — is one your newsroom will genuinely need as model-assisted drafting spreads. But this implementation is dormant and routes your unpublished copy through OpenAI, which is the wrong trade for a newsroom. I would implement the same check internally: extract claims with a self-hosted model, verify against your own document archive and a controlled search path, and keep the draft inside the building. Keep FacTool as a design reference.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2024-08-19, no releases, no tags, 937 stars, 24 open issues. Over two years inactive with an open backlog.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive; third-party API terms govern actual use.
costs: Software free; operation requires paid OpenAI and search API keys (rates not verified here). Per-use cost scales with document length.
privacy: NOT local — submitted text, extracted claims and generated search queries go to the configured LLM provider and search API. Unsuitable for unpublished copy about sensitive subjects.
alternatives: A self-hosted LLM performing claim extraction, with verification against your own archive
Loki for a similar pipeline — equally dormant and equally hosted-API dependent
Editorial process: a second human reading the draft against sources, which remains the reliable control
blockers: Requires hosted LLM and search APIs
summary: Framework for detecting factual errors in generated text across scenarios (knowledge-based QA, code, maths…

name: CooRTweet
purpose: R package that detects coordinated sharing behaviour in social-media data by finding accounts repeatedly posting the same content within a short time window, and builds the resulting co-sharing network.
journalism_use_case: Investigating whether a claim's apparent virality is organic or amplified: identify clusters of accounts pushing the same content in lockstep, which is a standard evidentiary step in disinformation-campaign reporting and one that holds up editorially when the method is stated.
pros: Platform-agnostic by design: analysis is fully local on data you already hold and the package does not call platform APIs — which is why it survived CrowdTangle's shutdown while CooRnet did not
Implements a published, citable method, so a story can state the parameters (time window, repetition threshold) and be reproduced
Active maintenance (pushed 2026-11-08) under MIT, with a tiny issue backlog
Outputs a network you can inspect in Gephi or igraph, making the finding visual and checkable rather than a single statistic
cons: Detects statistical co-occurrence, not intent — a cluster may be a campaign, a fan community, a newsletter or an artefact of the sampling window, and the method cannot distinguish these
You must supply the social-media data yourself, which after the platform API withdrawals is now the hard part of the whole workflow
Results are highly sensitive to the chosen time window and repetition threshold; different defensible parameters produce different networks, so parameter choices must be published
R-based, which is a mismatch if your stack is Python/TypeScript, and GitHub reports NOASSERTION for the licence although the project states MIT
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: active commits through 2026-11-08 with 57 stars and 1 open issue; the method derives from published coordinated-behaviour research. CooRnet's archival (same research area, CrowdTangle-dependent) is the instructive contrast and is verified in this catalogue.
assessment: The right tool for this analysis today, precisely because it is data-source agnostic. For your profile the binding constraint is not the tool but data acquisition — budget your effort there. Two editorial disciplines are non-negotiable: publish the parameters, and corroborate any cluster with non-statistical evidence (account creation patterns, shared infrastructure, content provenance) before characterising it as coordinated.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-08, no release objects, 57 stars, 1 open issue. Current commits from an active academic maintainer; note GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION while the project states MIT, so the licence label here rests on the project's own declaration.
licence: MIT (project-stated; GitHub API reports SPDX NOASSERTION)
licence_restrictions: None material, but the SPDX mismatch means confirm the LICENSE file before redistributing.
costs: No fee. Runs on a laptop in R. The real cost is obtaining social-media data — which after platform API restrictions may require paid research access, scraping (with its own legal and operational risk), or partnership with an academic data holder. Not priced here.
privacy: Analysis is fully local on data you already hold; the package makes no platform API calls. Data acquisition is the step with privacy and legal implications, not the analysis.
alternatives: CooRnet — archived, reference only
4CAT plus Zeeschuimer for data collection to feed this analysis
Gephi or igraph for visualising and interrogating the resulting network
summary: R package that detects coordinated sharing behaviour in social-media data by finding accounts repeatedly posting the same content…

name: CooRnet
purpose: R package that detected coordinated link-sharing behaviour across Facebook and Instagram using CrowdTangle data, producing co-sharing networks of pages and groups.
journalism_use_case: Historically the standard tool for showing that a false claim was amplified by a coordinated page network; now relevant mainly for reproducing or auditing published investigations that used it.
pros: Established the methodology that CooRTweet and successors implement, and remains the citation for a body of published investigations
MIT licensed with a clean reference implementation of coordinated link-sharing detection
Zero open issues at archival — it was a finished, working tool for its data source
cons: ARCHIVED and functionally dead: GitHub API confirms archived=true with last push 2024-08-14, which coincides with CrowdTangle's shutdown — its only data source no longer exists
Even with a data substitute, the package's assumptions are CrowdTangle-shaped (page/group entities, specific field names)
Facebook/Instagram only, so it never covered the platforms where much coordination now occurs
Its fate is a general warning: tools built on a single proprietary platform API inherit that API's lifespan
feedback: No individual user reports verified. The documented decisive facts: archived=true per the GitHub API on 2026-11-17, and the alignment of its final push (2024-08-14) with the discontinuation of the CrowdTangle data source it depended on.
assessment: Reference only, and a useful cautionary case for your planning: the single most consequential dependency in social-media research is not the library but the data source, and proprietary research APIs have been withdrawn repeatedly. Use CooRTweet, which is data-source agnostic, and design any monitoring you build so the collection layer can be replaced without rewriting the analysis.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=true, pushed_at 2024-08-14, no releases, 75 stars, 0 open issues. Archived by the maintainer; the underlying CrowdTangle API was discontinued, so the data layer is gone as well as the code being frozen.
licence_restrictions: None, but the code is frozen and inoperable.
costs: No fee. Not operable — CrowdTangle, its required data source, is shut down.
privacy: Historically sent URL lists to Meta's CrowdTangle API; now inoperable.
alternatives: CooRTweet — the recommended, data-source-agnostic successor
4CAT for collection plus network analysis on platforms that remain accessible
Published methodology papers for citing the method without running the code
blockers: Archived, and its sole data source (CrowdTangle) was discontinued
summary: R package that detected coordinated link-sharing behaviour across Facebook and Instagram using CrowdTangle data…

name: Full Fact AI Trust Benchmark
purpose: Benchmark and evaluation harness, authored by a fact-checking organisation, for assessing whether AI assistants behave acceptably on fact-checking-adjacent tasks.
journalism_use_case: Gives a newsroom a practitioner-authored rather than vendor-authored basis for deciding whether an AI assistant is fit to be placed near editorial fact-checking work — the question editors actually ask when a tool is pitched to them.
pros: Authored by working fact-checkers, so the evaluation criteria reflect editorial requirements rather than benchmark convenience — a genuinely different and useful perspective
Apache-2.0 and recently active (pushed 2026-11-03), so it reflects current model behaviour rather than a 2023 snapshot
Evaluates third-party models and distributes none, so there is no model-licence complication
cons: Very low adoption signal (3 stars, 0 open issues) and early-stage: this is a published artefact rather than an established standard, and its results have not been widely replicated
A benchmark, not a fact-checking tool — it tells you about a model, not about a claim
Scores are probabilistic snapshots of specific model versions and go stale quickly as providers update models silently
Running it sends benchmark prompts to the model providers under evaluation, which is inherent to the design but means your evaluation activity is visible to vendors
feedback: No individual user reports verified — the 3-star count means there is effectively no community signal to report, which I note rather than inflate. Full Fact's institutional standing in fact-checking is well established; this specific artefact is new.
assessment: Worth knowing about disproportionately to its adoption, because it is the only practitioner-authored evaluation in this catalogue and it answers a question your editors will ask. For your profile I would use its criteria as a checklist when assessing an AI tool rather than necessarily running the harness, and re-run or re-read it whenever you change model providers. Treat the specific scores as perishable.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-03, no releases, 3 stars, 0 open issues. Recent activity from an institutional maintainer; too new and too small to classify as actively maintained with confidence, and clearly not declining.
model_or_data_licence: n/a — evaluates third-party models and distributes none.
costs: No software fee. Running it incurs the API charges of whichever models you benchmark (rates vary by provider and were not verified here). Cost is proportional to the number of models and prompts.
privacy: Benchmark prompts are sent to the model providers under evaluation — inherent to the design. No sensitive material need be involved if you use the supplied prompts.
alternatives: AVeriTeC's evaluation design for a research-grade methodology — licence unconfirmed
Building a newsroom-specific evaluation set from your own published fact-checks
FEVER's annotation platform for constructing that set
summary: Benchmark and evaluation harness, authored by a fact-checking organisation, for assessing whether AI assistants behave acceptably…

name: Google Fact Check Tools API
purpose: Hosted API with a Claim Search endpoint for querying fact-checks published worldwide as ClaimReview structured data, plus a write API for submitting your own ClaimReview markup.
journalism_use_case: Check whether a circulating claim has already been fact-checked by any publisher worldwide before spending desk time on it, and publish your own fact-checks as structured ClaimReview so they are discoverable by others — the two halves of not duplicating work.
pros: By far the broadest coverage of published fact-checks available through one interface, because it aggregates ClaimReview markup globally
The write side matters strategically: emitting ClaimReview makes your own fact-checks discoverable and citable by other desks and by search surfaces
No infrastructure to operate, and the lookup is fast enough for live use during a breaking story
cons: NOT open source: a hosted service under Google's API Terms, with deprecation and quota risk entirely outside your control — the same class of dependency that killed CooRnet
Coverage is limited to publishers emitting valid ClaimReview markup, which skews toward larger and English-language organisations and silently under-represents smaller and non-Western fact-checkers
Queries and submitted markup go to Google, so your checking activity on a sensitive subject is visible to a third party
Licence and current pricing/quota terms were not verified in this survey — treat both as unconfirmed here
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented from the project's own documentation: API users must inform their own users that results come from the Fact Check Tools API, and coverage depends on publisher ClaimReview emission. Quota and pricing details were not verified in this survey.
assessment: Use it, with eyes open about what it is: a convenience layer over other people's structured markup, operated by a company that has retired APIs before. For your profile the asymmetry is worth noting — the write side (publishing ClaimReview) has lasting value independent of Google, because the markup is a standard; the read side is a dependency. I would emit ClaimReview regardless and treat the lookup as a useful but replaceable step, with a manual search fallback documented.
maintenance_evidence: No repository to inspect. The service was live and documented at developers.google.com/fact-check/tools/api as of this survey, but I did not verify current quota, pricing or deprecation status from the vendor in this session. Classified Uncertain deliberately: a hosted API's maintenance cannot be evidenced the way a repository's can, and Google's API deprecation record justifies caution rather than an assumption of continuity.
licence: Not applicable (hosted service under Google API Terms of Service); specific terms not verified in this survey
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Note that the underlying ClaimReview content belongs to the publishing fact-checkers.
licence_restrictions: Service terms rather than a software licence. Documentation states an attribution obligation to end users. Republishing aggregated fact-check content raises the publishers' own rights, separate from Google's terms.
costs: Pricing and quota NOT verified in this survey — treat as not publicly confirmed here and check the current terms before relying on it. Historically free within quota; a Google API key is required, and Search Console verification is required for the ClaimReview write API.
privacy: Queries and submitted ClaimReview markup go to Google. Your lookup activity discloses which claims you are examining, which is a consideration if the subject is sensitive or if the target might observe published queries indirectly.
alternatives: Emitting ClaimReview markup yourself regardless of the read API
ClaimsKG extractor for a self-hosted database — but dormant and unlicensed
Manual search across the major fact-checking sites as a documented fallback
blockers: Hosted proprietary API with deprecation and quota risk outside your control; terms and pricing unverified in this survey
summary: Hosted API with a Claim Search endpoint for querying fact-checks published worldwide as ClaimReview structured data…
oss_detail: Hosted service or proprietary software — governed by service terms, not a software licence

name: PhotoHolmes
purpose: Python library that packages multiple published image-forgery detection and localisation methods behind a common interface, with preprocessing, benchmarking and a plugin structure for adding methods.
journalism_use_case: Lets an engineer embedded in a verification team run several published localisation methods over one contested image and compare heatmaps, rather than trusting a single model — and, just as usefully, benchmark honestly how badly each method degrades on recompressed social-media copies.
pros: Method ensembling with a common interface is the correct epistemic approach to image forensics: agreement across independent methods is informative, a single heatmap is not
The benchmarking capability lets you measure degradation on platform-recompressed images, which is the condition that actually matters and which papers rarely report
Apache-2.0 for the harness, and the README explicitly flags that bundled methods carry their own terms — honest licence signposting that is rare in research code
cons: Apache-2.0 covers the harness only: individual methods carry their own, sometimes non-commercial licences, and the README specifically flags TruFor as restricted to non-profit use — so the ensemble as a whole may not be commercially usable
Outputs are probabilistic localisation maps and scores from research models, NOT conclusive proof of manipulation; heatmaps are highly suggestive to non-experts and easy to over-read
Low activity (pushed 2026-01-05, no releases, 53 stars) and a small academic team — you would own maintenance
Per-method pretrained weights are fetched from third-party hosts (HuggingFace, authors' links), which is a supply-chain and availability risk
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the README's own licence warnings about bundled methods (including TruFor's non-profit restriction); 53 stars with 3 open issues; last push 2026-01-05.
assessment: The right structure for forensic work and worth adopting if you have an engineer who can own it — the per-method licence audit is the task to do first, method by method, before anything reaches publication. For your profile the pragmatic configuration is to enable only the permissively licensed methods and accept a smaller ensemble, since a non-commercial method's output in a commercially published story is a licence breach. Every output is a lead requiring non-forensic corroboration.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-01-05, no releases or tags, 53 stars, 3 open issues. Ten months since last push; small academic project with a complete initial release. Not classified declining because the harness is functionally complete and the issue count is low, but there is no evidence of ongoing work.
model_or_data_licence: Varies per bundled method; the README flags TruFor as restricted to non-profit use. Several bundled methods carry non-OSI academic terms.
licence_restrictions: Material: the harness is permissive but the methods inside it are not uniformly so. A commercial newsroom must audit and selectively disable methods. Do not treat the Apache-2.0 badge as covering the ensemble.
costs: No fee. GPU helpful for some methods; per-method weights downloaded from third-party hosts. Cost is engineer time for the licence audit and integration. Estimate.
privacy: Inference is local, so case images need not leave the newsroom — a significant advantage over the InVID plugin's forensics panels. Weight downloads from third-party hosts are the only external touchpoint and can be pre-staged.
alternatives: Sherloq for a GUI workbench usable by a non-engineer, fully local
CAT-Net for JPEG-specific splicing detection with CC-BY-4.0 weights
TruFor for reliability-mapped localisation — but non-commercial licence only
blockers: Bundled methods carry mixed and partly non-commercial licences — per-method audit required before commercial publication
summary: Python library that packages multiple published image-forgery detection and localisation methods behind a common interface…

name: TruFor
purpose: Transformer-based image-forgery localisation model combining learned noise-residual fingerprints with RGB features, producing both a manipulation heatmap and a confidence/reliability map.
journalism_use_case: Second-opinion localisation on a single contested photo, where the reliability map is used to discount regions in which the model is unreliable — useful precisely because it tempers false alarms rather than producing a bare score.
pros: The reliability map is a genuine methodological advance for journalism: it tells you where not to trust the heatmap, which reduces the chance of publishing a false manipulation claim
Strong published performance among localisation methods, from a group with a long forensics research record
Inference runs locally inside Docker, so contested images need not leave the newsroom
cons: NOT open source: LICENSE.txt restricts use to informational and non-profit purposes, copyright GRIP-UNINA — a legal problem for any commercially operated newsroom and a blocker that is easy to miss because the code is on GitHub
Outputs are probabilistic forensic signals, never conclusive proof of manipulation; platform recompression substantially degrades the signal
Low activity (pushed 2025-05-29, no releases, 287 stars, 11 open issues) — a research release rather than a maintained tool
Docker plus specific PyTorch versions; weights obtained per repository instructions rather than a package manager
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the LICENSE.txt restriction to informational and non-profit use, read in session 1 and retained; PhotoHolmes independently flags TruFor's non-profit restriction in its own README, which corroborates the reading.
assessment: Technically among the best available and legally unusable for a commercial newsroom without permission — that combination is the whole assessment. For your profile: if you work with a non-profit outlet or a research partner, this is a strong second opinion; if the outlet is commercially operated, either seek written permission from GRIP-UNINA or use CAT-Net, whose weights are CC-BY-4.0. Do not assume 'journalism is informational' satisfies an informational-use clause intended to exclude commercial deployment.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2025-05-29, no releases or tags, SPDX none, 287 stars, 11 open issues. Eighteen months since last push; a published research artefact that is complete rather than evolving.
licence: NOT OSS — custom GRIP-UNINA terms: LICENSE.txt restricts use to informational and non-profit purposes
model_or_data_licence: Same custom non-commercial GRIP-UNINA terms apply to the weights.
licence_restrictions: Commercial use is not permitted without separate permission. 'Informational and non-profit' does not clearly cover a commercially published investigation, and should not be assumed to. Redistribution is similarly restricted.
costs: No fee for permitted non-profit/informational use. Commercial use requires permission — terms not publicly listed. GPU and Docker for inference.
privacy: Inference is local inside Docker, so images need not leave the newsroom. No third-party service documented.
alternatives: CAT-Net — CC-BY-4.0 weights, commercially usable, JPEG-focused
PhotoHolmes to run several methods including permissive ones
Sherloq for a fully local, GPL-3.0 manual forensics workbench
blockers: Licence restricts use to informational and non-profit purposes — commercial newsroom use requires permission
summary: Transformer-based image-forgery localisation model combining learned noise-residual fingerprints with RGB features…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: CAT-Net
purpose: Neural network that detects and localises spliced regions in JPEG images by tracing compression-artefact inconsistencies, using both RGB and DCT-domain streams.
journalism_use_case: Spotting spliced-in regions in JPEGs that still retain their original compression history — for example a photo circulated as a camera original rather than a platform re-encode, where a pasted element carries a different compression signature from its surroundings.
pros: CC-BY-4.0 pretrained weights and Apache-2.0 code per the README licence section — a commercially usable combination, which is rare among forensic models and is the main reason to prefer it over TruFor
Compression-artefact tracing is a physically grounded signal rather than a learned style cue, so a positive finding is more explainable to an editor
Still receiving commits (pushed 2026-10-15) years after publication
cons: Depends on JPEG compression artefacts, so its signal is weak or absent for PNGs, screenshots and heavily re-encoded images — which is the state most social-media images arrive in, sharply limiting real-world applicability
v1 handles splicing only, not other manipulation classes, so a negative result says very little
Pretrained and trained weights are hosted on Google Drive and Baiduyun — an availability and supply-chain risk, and awkward for automated deployment
44 open issues against 317 stars with no releases or tags; GitHub reports no SPDX licence, so the Apache-2.0/CC-BY-4.0 position rests on the README rather than a detected licence file
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: the README licence section stating Apache-2.0 code and CC-BY-4.0 weights and datasets (read in session 1, retained); weights hosted on Google Drive and Baiduyun; 317 stars with 44 open issues.
assessment: The commercially usable forensic localisation model in this catalogue, which makes it the default choice for a commercial newsroom despite TruFor's technical edge. Its real limitation is scope: it answers a narrow question about JPEG splicing, and the images you most want to check have usually been recompressed past the point where it helps. Use it when you have what purports to be a camera original, mirror the weights locally rather than depending on Google Drive, and treat output as a lead.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-15, no releases or tags, SPDX none, 317 stars, 44 open issues. Commits within the last month but no release engineering and a sizeable backlog; a research artefact receiving occasional attention.
licence: Apache-2.0 (code), per the README licence section; GitHub API reports no detected licence
model_or_data_licence: CC-BY-4.0 for pretrained weights and released datasets, per the README licence section.
licence_restrictions: CC-BY-4.0 requires attribution — cite the model in any methodology note. No non-commercial restriction, which is the key advantage. Because GitHub detects no licence file, confirm the README statement against the repository before commercial reliance.
costs: No fee. GPU for inference. Weights from third-party file hosts (mirror them). Estimate.
privacy: Weights pulled from Google Drive/Baiduyun on setup; inference is local thereafter, so contested images stay in the newsroom.
alternatives: TruFor for stronger localisation — but non-commercial licence only
PhotoHolmes to compare several methods including this one
Sherloq's JPEG ghost and ELA panels for a quicker manual check
summary: Neural network that detects and localises spliced regions in JPEG images by tracing compression-artefact inconsistencies…

name: UniversalFakeDetect
purpose: Method and reference implementation showing that a linear classifier on frozen CLIP features generalises across image generators better than purpose-trained detectors, with evaluation sets across many generator families.
journalism_use_case: A baseline for teams testing whether any synthetic-image detector holds up on their own case material — valuable mainly as the honest yardstick for cross-generator generalisation claims, which is the axis on which vendor detectors fail.
pros: The finding itself is the value: a simple CLIP-feature classifier generalising better than specialised detectors is a strong reason to distrust vendor claims about bespoke detection models
MIT licensed with author-distributed weights, so it can be run and cited freely
Evaluation across many generator families makes it a usable generalisation test rather than a single-generator demo
cons: A score is a probabilistic signal, NOT evidence or proof that an image was AI-generated — and because the method is simple, non-experts over-trust it

The repository notes that its released diffusion evaluation set is reduced to 1k real / 1k fake per domain versus 10k in the paper, so published numbers are not reproducible from the release as distributed
Predates the current generation of image models, so its own generalisation claims need re-testing against 2025-2026 generators
Requires CLIP weights and author-hosted datasets of roughly 72GB across 20 categories — a substantial download; 24 open issues, no releases
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented from the repository itself: the reduced released evaluation set versus the paper (1k versus 10k per domain), which is an honest disclosure by the authors and a real reproducibility limit. 381 stars, 24 open issues, last push 2026-08-19.
assessment: Use it as a measuring stick, not a detector. Concretely, for your work: when someone offers an AI-image detector, test it and this baseline on the same set of images from generators neither has seen, and expect both to degrade sharply. The Deepfake-Eval-2024 finding (roughly 45-50% AUC drops in the wild) is the number to keep in mind. Never publish a synthetic-media claim on detector output alone.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-08-19, no releases or tags, 381 stars, 24 open issues. Three months since last push; a research release receiving light maintenance.
model_or_data_licence: Not separately stated; weights distributed by the authors under the repository terms. Evaluation datasets aggregate third-party generator outputs whose own terms may vary.
licence_restrictions: Code MIT. Residual uncertainty on the aggregated evaluation datasets, which include outputs from generators with their own terms of service.
costs: No fee. Roughly 72GB of dataset downloads plus CLIP weights; GPU for evaluation. Bandwidth and storage are the notable costs. Estimate.
privacy: Dataset and CLIP weight downloads from third-party hosts; classification runs locally, so case images stay in the newsroom.
alternatives: Community Forensics for a broader-training-distribution open baseline with MIT weights
Deepfake-Eval-2024 for the in-the-wild degradation figures to cite
Non-forensic verification — provenance, reverse search, source contact — which remains more reliable than any detector
summary: Method and reference implementation showing that a linear classifier on frozen CLIP features generalises across image generators…
